### Ch 43 — Ataxia, Paresis, and Paralysis
*(Author: Ronaldo Casimiro da Costa)*

#### Definitions
- **Ataxia**: incoordination; sensory (not motor) dysfunction; only identifiable when patient moves
- **Paresis**: partial loss of motor function (weakness)
- **Paralysis/Plegia**: complete loss of motor function

#### Three Types of Ataxia

**1. Vestibular Ataxia** (easiest to recognize)
- Head tilt (side of tilt = side of lesion usually)
- Other signs: leaning, falling, rolling, circling, strabismus, nystagmus
- **Peripheral vestibular**: NO change in mental status, NO proprioceptive deficits; nystagmus same direction, horizontal or rotatory (not vertical); idiopathic vestibular disease always peripheral
- **Central vestibular**: somnolence, proprioceptive/hopping deficits; vertical nystagmus or positional nystagmus; paradoxical: deficits contralateral to head tilt

**2. Cerebellar Ataxia**
- Dysmetria (inability to control rate/range of stepping); usually hypermetria in thoracic limbs
- Head tremors, intention tremors, wide pelvic limb stance/gait
- NO weakness, NO proprioceptive positioning deficits

**3. Proprioceptive Ataxia** (primary spinal cord sign)
- Truncal sway, circumduction, limb crossing; no head involvement
- Accompanied by CP deficits usually; chronic cases may have ataxia without CP deficits

#### DDx by Lesion Localization (Box 43.1)

**Vestibular Ataxia — Peripheral**
- Otitis media-interna
- Idiopathic vestibular disease
- Neoplasia

**Vestibular Ataxia — Central**
- Noninfectious meningoencephalitis (GME, NME, etc.)
- Infectious meningoencephalitis
- Neoplasia

**Cerebellar Ataxia**
- Noninfectious meningoencephalitis
- Infectious meningoencephalitis
- Cerebellar hypoplasia

**Proprioceptive Ataxia / Paresis (Spinal)**
- C1-C5: intervertebral disc disease, atlantoaxial subluxation, neoplasia
- C6-T2: IVDD, cervical spondylomyelopathy, neoplasia
- T3-L3: IVDD, spinal trauma, degenerative myelopathy, neoplasia, fibrocartilaginous embolism (FCE)
- L4-S3: IVDD, FCE, spinal trauma, neoplasia

**Diffuse Lower Motor Neuron Signs**
- Acute polyradiculoneuritis (Coonhound paralysis)
- Myasthenia gravis
- Botulism
- Tick paralysis

**Cauda Equina (L6, L7, Sacrum)**
- Degenerative lumbosacral stenosis
- Spinal trauma
- Discospondylitis
- Neoplasia

#### UMN vs LMN Signs
- **UMN**: paresis/paralysis + increased extensor tone (spasticity/hypertonus), normal-to-increased reflexes (hyperreflexia), slow disuse muscle atrophy
- **LMN**: paresis/paralysis + absent-to-decreased tone (flaccidity/hypotonus), decreased/absent reflexes (hyporeflexia/areflexia), rapid severe neurogenic muscle atrophy
- **Schiff-Sherrington** phenomenon: severe T2-L7 lesion; paraplegia with thoracic limb spasticity when laterally recumbent (due to loss of inhibitory propriospinal tract)
- **Spinal shock**: peracute T3-L3 myelopathy → first 24h: decreased tone and reflexes; after 24-48h: expected UMN signs emerge

#### Nociception Assessment
- Noxious stimulus (e.g., pinch toe) → limb withdrawal (spinal reflex) AND behavioral response (vocalization, looking) = intact nociception
- Limb withdrawal WITHOUT behavioral response = absent conscious pain perception = severe lesion → guarded-to-poor prognosis

### Ch 44 — Stupor and Coma
*(Author: Eileen Kenney)*

#### Definitions
- **Stupor**: rousable unconsciousness; animal can be aroused by noxious stimulus but lapses back when stimulus removed
- **Coma**: unrousable unconsciousness; cannot be aroused even by noxious stimulus
- Note: limb withdrawal from noxious stimulus = spinal reflex, NOT consciousness
- **ARAS**: ascending reticular activating system (pontine/midbrain); modulates arousal; consciousness requires both ARAS and cerebral cortex

#### Cushing Reflex (Cerebral Ischemic Response)
- Triggered by severe acute ICP increase
- Causes: systemic hypertension (to maintain CPP) + concurrent vagally-mediated reflex bradycardia
- Indicates life-threatening intracranial hypertension with imminent herniation → immediate treatment

#### Full DDx — Box 44.1: Causes of Stupor and Coma

**Structural**
- Traumatic brain injury
- Cerebrovascular accident (stroke)
- Infection/Inflammation: meningitis, encephalitis, abscess
- Neoplasia
- Hydrocephalus
- Demyelination

**Toxins**
- CNS depressants: opiates, benzodiazepines, muscle relaxants, sympatholytics, macrocyclic lactones, anticonvulsants, cannabinoids, antihistamines, alcohols (ethylene glycol)
- Heavy metals: lead, mercury, aluminum
- Cellular hypoxia: carbon monoxide, cyanide, methemoglobinemia (e.g., acetaminophen)
- Cerebral edema: bromethalin

**Metabolic**
- Hypoperfusion
- Hypertensive encephalopathy
- Sepsis
- Hypo/hyperthermia
- Hyper/hypoglycemia
- Electrolyte disorders: hyper/hyponatremia, hyper/hypocalcemia, hypermagnesemia
- Acid/base derangements: acidosis, hypercarbia
- Organ system dysfunction: hepatic, kernicterus, renal, hypothyroid, adrenal insufficiency, cardiorespiratory
- Seizure-related: nonconvulsive status epilepticus, prolonged postictal states
- Nutritional deficiencies: thiamine, B12
- Anemia

#### Assessment: Neurological Examination Findings
**Pupil signs by lesion location:**
- Bilateral small reactive pupils → metabolic encephalopathy or bilateral diencephalic injury
- Pinpoint pupils → pontine injury (descending sympathetic destruction)
- Fixed dilated bilateral → CN III/midbrain damage bilaterally; or midposition if sympathetic tracts also absent
- Unilateral fixed pupil → ipsilateral midbrain lesion OR unilateral CN III compression (uncal herniation)

**Skeletal motor responses:**
- Decerebrate posture: extensor rigidity all 4 limbs; lesion in midbrain/rostral pons or bilateral cerebral hemispheric dysfunction; stupor/coma present
- Decerebellate posture: opisthotonos, forelimb extension, pelvic/hindlimb flexion; does NOT affect consciousness

**Respiratory patterns:**
- Kussmaul: rapid, deep, labored → severe metabolic acidosis
- Cheyne-Stokes: cyclical apnea-hyperpnea → diencephalon/pons lesion or bilateral cerebral hemisphere dysfunction
- Central neurogenic hyperventilation: persistent deep rapid breathing → pons/medulla lesion
- Apneustic breathing: prolonged inspiration with breath hold → upper pons (pneumotaxic center damage)
- Ataxic respiration: completely irregular → medulla damage → intubate immediately
- Agonal breathing: shallow gasps from anoxic injury → rapidly progresses to apnea/death

#### Treatment
- Mannitol, hypertonic saline for cerebral edema (if traumatic brain injury excluded → injectable corticosteroids also); not corticosteroids in TBI
- Head elevation 30° reduces ICP by facilitating venous drainage
- Hyperventilation to PaCO₂ ~30 mm Hg (brief only; limits cerebral blood flow)
- Modified Glasgow Coma Scale for serial assessment

### Ch 45 — Seizures
*(Author: Karen R. Muñana)*

#### Definitions
- Prevalence: 0.82% dogs; up to 0.16% cats
- **Generalized seizures**: abnormal neuronal activity from both hemispheres at onset; tonic-clonic, loss of consciousness, autonomic signs; also myoclonic and atonic seizures
- **Focal seizures**: discrete region of cerebrum/thalamus; focal motor activity, autonomic signs, behavioral abnormalities; can secondarily generalize
- **Epilepsy**: ≥2 unprovoked seizures ≥24 hours apart; enduring predisposition
- **Idiopathic epilepsy**: genetic predisposition; no other underlying cause; diagnosed in >50% of dogs with recurrent seizures (ages 6 months–6 years)
- **Structural epilepsy**: congenital or acquired lesion (hydrocephalus, encephalitis, CVD, trauma, neoplasia)
- **Epilepsy of unknown cause**: genetic unlikely based on age/findings but structural cause not identified; or full workup not performed
- **Reactive seizures**: extracranial causes (metabolic/toxic); brain otherwise healthy; NOT epilepsy

#### Clinical Features of Seizures vs Other Episodic Disorders (Table 45.1)
- **Seizures**: abnormal pre-episode behavior (prodrome); post-ictal period (fatigue, disorientation, aggression, compulsive walking, blindness; minutes to days); precipitating event: often REST; IMPAIRED consciousness; INCREASED tone; autonomic signs often present
- **Syncope**: immediate return to normal; precipitating event: exercise/excitement/none; LOSS of consciousness (brief); typically FLACCID; possible abnormal heart rate/urination
- **Narcolepsy/cataplexy**: precipitating event: excitement, eating; loss of consciousness (asleep) with narcolepsy, FLACCID; no autonomic signs
- **Transient vestibular**: normal; seconds to hours
- **Behavioral**: normal; possible environmental triggers; minutes to hours
- **Idiopathic head tremor**: normal; none; seconds to minutes
- **Paroxysmal movement disorders**: normal; none or exercise/excitement; increased tone; NO autonomic signs

#### Cats with Focal Seizures
- Orofacial motor signs: lip smacking, chewing, licking, swallowing; behavioral: vocalization, piloerection, aggression, motionless staring, startling/running
- May not be immediately recognized as seizures; associated with specific cat epilepsy syndrome

#### Full DDx — Box 45.1

**Extracranial Causes — Reactive Seizures**
- Metabolic: hepatic encephalopathy, renal/uremic encephalopathy, hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, sodium imbalance, hyperlipoproteinemia, thiamine deficiency
- Toxic: heavy metals, pesticides, ethylene glycol, caffeine/methylxanthines, mycotoxins, drugs

**Intracranial Causes — Structural Epilepsy**
- Degenerative: neurodegenerative disorders, lysosomal storage disorders
- Anomalous: hydrocephalus, lissencephaly, cortical malformations
- Neoplastic: primary, metastatic
- Infectious: viral, bacterial, protozoal, rickettsial, fungal/algal, parasitic
- Inflammatory: meningoencephalitis of unknown etiology (granulomatous, necrotizing)
- Traumatic: brain trauma
- Vascular: cerebrovascular disease, systemic hypertension

**Idiopathic Epilepsy**: genetic (proven or presumed)

**Epilepsy of Unknown Cause**: no structural cause identified

#### Diagnostic Approach by Age (Dogs)
- **6 months–6 years**: high probability idiopathic epilepsy (up to 75% of this age group); work up extracranial causes first; if negative → Tier I: presumptive idiopathic epilepsy; Tier II: requires MRI + CSF
- **<6 months**: idiopathic epilepsy still most likely; but structural (brain anomalies, infectious) also high probability → more extensive workup warranted; ultrasound through open fontanelle for ventriculomegaly
- **>6–7 years**: structural epilepsy most likely; neoplasia most common in older dogs; serial blood pressure measurements; thoracic radiographs + abdominal ultrasound to screen; MRI + CSF if unremarkable

#### Cats
- Structural epilepsy diagnosed in up to 2/3 of cats with recurrent seizures (vs dogs where idiopathic is majority)
- MRI + CSF recommended for all cats with recurrent seizures regardless of age
- Cats with infectious disease: test for FIV, FeLV, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis
- Idiopathic epilepsy occurs but proportionally less frequent

#### Red Flags → Structural Workup
- Onset <6 months or >6 years
- Neurological abnormalities between episodes
- Progressive increase in frequency/severity
- Cluster seizures or status epilepticus

> ClinIQ: maps to Seizures

### Ch 46 — Halitosis and Ptyalism
*(Author: Lenin Arturo Villamizar Martinez)*

#### Halitosis

**Definition**: Acute or chronic offensive odor from intra- or extraoral origin. Volatile sulfur compounds (VSCs) and proteolytic byproducts (cadaverine, putrescine, indole, skatole) produced by bacteria.

**Most common cause**: Periodontal disease (prevalence 44–100% in dogs under GA depending on study)

**Full DDx — Fig 46.2**

*Intraoral*
- Periodontal disease (gingivitis, dental calculus, gum recession, furcation exposure, periodontal pockets)
- Oral neoplasia
- Inflammatory/ulcerative conditions:
  - Feline chronic gingivostomatitis
  - Canine chronic ulcerative gingivostomatitis
  - Canine contact stomatitis
  - Eosinophilic granuloma complex
  - Immune-mediated oral lesions (pemphigus vulgaris, bullous pemphigoid, lupus erythematosus, mucous membrane pemphigoid)
  - Chemical/thermal mucositis
  - Uremic ulcers
- Idiopathic osteonecrosis or osteoradionecrosis of the jaw
- Palatitis in brachycephalic breeds (food debris/hair/bacteria in deep rugae)
- Foreign body
- Ingestion of feces/trash/carrion; excessive licking of perianal area (anal sac disease)

*Extraoral*
- Lip fold dermatitis
- Digestive tract disease: megaesophagus, esophageal/gastric infectious or neoplastic process
- Upper/lower respiratory tract disease: nasopharyngeal infection, sinus infection, pneumonia, nasopharyngeal/lung cancer
- Systemic disorder:
  - Diabetes mellitus → sweet or fruity breath
  - Kidney disease → uremic breath
  - Liver disease → bad breath associated with vomiting

**Diagnosis**: Organoleptic assessment (smelling) or halimeter (portable VSC monitor)

#### Ptyalism

**Definition**: Overflow of saliva = increased saliva production OR inability to swallow/retain normal amounts

**Physiologic ptyalism**: sensory stimulation (sight, hearing, smell, taste), food mastication, thermoregulation, drug effect (e.g., ketamine)

**Full DDx — Fig 46.4**

*Excessive saliva production*
- Salivary gland disease: sialocele, sialadenitis, sialadenosis, necrotizing sialometaplasia, neoplasia
- Inflammatory oral conditions: gingivostomatitis (cats), severe periodontal disease, mucositis/bone necrosis, autoimmune oral lesions, eosinophilic granuloma, uremic ulcers, trauma
- Infectious diseases: calicivirus, candidiasis
- Oropharyngeal cancer
- Portosystemic shunt (more frequent in cats)
- Megaesophagus
- Pain

*Inability to swallow/retain saliva*
- Inability to close mouth: trigeminal neuropathy, open-mouth jaw locking, mandibular fracture
- Oropharyngeal foreign body
- Inflammatory/neoplastic/neurologic disorders affecting the tongue
- Rabies (zoonotic — key differential with neurologic signs; seizures, paralysis, fever, behavioral changes)
- Abnormal lip conformation (Saint Bernard, Mastiff, Newfoundland, Basset Hound)

> ClinIQ: no matching sign screen (candidate — Ptyalism/Drooling)

### Ch 47 — Gagging and Dysphagia
*(Author: Megan Grobman)*

#### Definitions
- **Dysphagia**: swallowing impairment; clinical finding not diagnosis
- **Gagging**: airway protective behavior; stimulated by touching base of tongue, palate, epiglottis, caudal pharynx; CN V (sensory afferent) → CN X (efferent)
- **Retching**: unsuccessful attempt to expel gastric contents; rhythmic heaving; functions: trigger vomiting, provide rostral momentum, mix/buffer gastric contents
- **Expectoration**: clearance of mucoid secretions from airways; "hacking" mistaken for gagging/retching; terminal retch at end of coughing paroxysm suggests respiratory disease

#### Swallowing Phases
1. **Oral preparatory** (voluntary): prehension, mastication, bolus formation
2. **Pharyngeal/cricopharyngeal** (involuntary): food bolus through upper esophageal sphincter
3. **Esophageal/gastroesophageal** (involuntary): primary peristalsis → LES relaxation

#### Full DDx — Table 47.2

**Gagging (respiratory causes)**
- Nasal: nasopharyngeal mass or FB
- Upper airway: pharyngeal collapse, epiglottic retroversion, laryngeal paralysis
- Lower airway: productive or severe cough of multiple etiologies

**Dysphagia**

*Oral Preparatory*
- Mechanical: periodontal disease, FB, oral mass/swelling, sialadenosis/sialadenitis, oral/facial trauma, cleft palate, TMJ disorder, stomatitis, retrobulbar abscess
- Functional: CN V, VII, XII dysfunction; masticatory myositis; trigeminal neuritis; IMPA; lingual myositis/glossitis; polymyositis

*Pharyngeal (including cricopharyngeal)*
- Mechanical: neoplasia, FB, tonsillar swelling, elongated soft palate, pharyngeal abscess/trauma, nasopharyngeal polyp, mucocele, disruption of hyoid apparatus, retropharyngeal lymphadenopathy
- Functional: CN IX, X, XI dysfunction; cricopharyngeal achalasia or dyssynchrony; extra-esophageal reflux disease (EERD); myasthenia gravis (MG); polyradiculoneuritis; tetanus; GOLPP; hypophosphatemia; hypocalcemia; rabies; pseudorabies; polymyositis; hypoadrenocorticism; dystrophin deficiency

*Esophageal (including gastroesophageal)*
- Mechanical: FB, vascular ring anomaly, stricture, diverticulum, neoplasia, hiatal hernia, gastroesophageal intussusception, spirocercosis, pythiosis, trauma
- Functional: CN X or diffuse autonomic dysfunction, dysautonomia, GERD, idiopathic esophageal dysmotility (IED), primary or secondary megaesophagus, LES achalasia-like syndrome (LES-AS), esophagitis, botulism, tetanus, distemper, MG, hypothyroidism, hypoadrenocorticism, lead intoxication, thallium intoxication, acetylcholinesterase inhibitor intoxication, polymyositis, polyneuritis, polyradiculoneuritis, glycogen storage disease, trypanosomiasis, dystrophin deficiency

#### Breed/Familial Predispositions (Table 47.3)
- **Dystrophin deficiency**: Belgian Shepherd, Brittany Spaniel, German Shorthaired Pointer, Golden Retriever, Irish Terrier, Japanese Spitz, Miniature Schnauzer, Rat Terrier, Rottweiler
- **Cricopharyngeal achalasia**: Cocker Spaniel, Golden Retriever
- **IED**: Bouvier des Flandres, Chinese Shar-Pei, terriers
- **Vascular ring anomalies**: German Shepherd Dog, Irish Setter
- **Gastroesophageal intussusception**: German Shepherd Dog
- **Hiatal hernia**: Brachycephalic breeds, Chinese Shar-Pei
- **Hereditary megaesophagus**: Miniature Schnauzer, Wire-Haired Fox Terrier
- **Congenital megaesophagus**: Chinese Shar-Pei, GSD, Great Dane, Irish Setter, Labrador Retriever, Newfoundland
- **Familial megaesophagus**: GSD, Great Dane, Irish Setter, Newfoundland, Siamese cat

#### Diagnostic Gold Standard
- Videofluoroscopic Swallow Studies (VFSS): free-feeding, free-standing protocol preferred; criterion standard
- LES-AS identified in subpopulation of dogs with esophageal dysphagia → responds to targeted intervention (balloon dilation, botulinum toxin A, surgical myotomy + fundoplication)
- Thoracic radiographs (minimum 3 views) in all patients with dysphagia to identify megaesophagus and aspiration pneumonia

### Ch 48 — Regurgitation and Vomiting
*(Author: Alex Gallagher)*

#### Definitions and Differentiation (Table 48.1)
| Feature | Regurgitation | Vomiting |
|---|---|---|
| Nausea/hypersalivation | No | Common |
| Retching/abdominal contractions | No | Common |
| Presence of bile | Rare | +/- |
| Cervical esophageal distension | +/- | No |
| Amount | Any | Any |
| Time after eating | Variable | Variable |
| pH | Variable | Variable |

- **Regurgitation**: passive expulsion from pharynx or esophagus; no abdominal contractions; animal simply lowers head and material falls out; mucus or bile rare (reflux from stomach into esophagus possible)
- **Vomiting**: active centrally-mediated reflex; prodromal nausea, lip-smacking; retching; closures of nasopharynx and glottis to protect airway; bile indicates patency of gastric outflow
- **Vomiting food >8 hours post-ingestion**: suggests delayed gastric emptying (obstruction or hypomotility)
- Regurgitation uncommon in cats → assume vomiting in cats unless otherwise confirmed
- pH not reliable differentiator

#### Regurgitation — Common Causes
- Megaesophagus (primary: idiopathic/hereditary; secondary: MG, hypothyroidism, hypoadrenocorticism, lead intox)
- Esophagitis
- Foreign body
- Vascular ring anomaly
- Stricture
- Diverticulum
- Neoplasia
- Hiatal hernia

#### Vomiting Pathophysiology
- Emetic center: medullary nucleus group; serotonergic (5HT1) + alpha2 adrenergic receptors; adjacent NK1 receptors in nucleus tractus solitarii
- **CRTZ** (area postrema; no blood-brain barrier): D2, H1, alpha2, 5HT3, M1, enkephalinergic (ENK-mu, delta), NK1 receptors → samples blood for toxins/drugs
- Species difference: apomorphine (D1+D2 agonist) = potent emetic in dogs but NOT cats; xylazine (alpha2 agonist) = effective emetic in cats; cisplatin-induced emesis in dogs = visceral rather than central 5HT3 receptors

#### Common Causes of Vomiting (Box 48.1)

*Metabolic Diseases*
- Renal disease
- Hepatobiliary disease or failure
- Electrolyte derangements
- Acid-base derangements
- Endotoxemia

*Endocrine Diseases*
- Hypoadrenocorticism
- Hyperthyroidism

*Toxins/Drugs*
- Heavy metals
- Ethylene glycol
- NSAIDs
- Antibiotics
- Chemotherapy agents

*Dietary Causes*
- Dietary indiscretion
- Allergy
- Intolerance

*Abdominal Diseases*
- Pancreatitis
- Peritonitis
- Neoplasia

*Gastric Diseases*
- Gastritis
- Parasites
- Helicobacter
- Foreign bodies
- Obstruction
- GDV
- Motility disorders
- Neoplasia

*Small Intestinal Diseases*
- IBD
- Neoplasia
- Obstruction
- Parasites
- Infections

*Large Intestinal Diseases*
- Constipation
- Colitis

#### Diagnostic Approach
**Acute, mild**: fecal exam ± radiographs → if parasites: anthelmintic; if nonspecific gastroenteritis: supportive (withhold food 12–24h, ± fluids, ± anti-emetics); if severe/life-threatening signs: CBC, biochemistry, urinalysis, fecal exam, radiographs ± ultrasound → treat underlying cause (GDV, FB, obstruction, peritonitis = surgery; metabolic = specific therapy)

**Chronic (>1–2 weeks)**: CBC, biochemistry, urinalysis, T4 (cats), fecal exam, radiographs; cats: FeLV/FIV; cats >5 years: thyroid T4; additional: ultrasound, heartworm test (cats), bile acids, pancreatic lipase, ACTH stimulation; diet trial (stable: hypoallergenic, highly digestible); endoscopic or surgical biopsy (chronic gastritis, Helicobacter, IBD, neoplasia)

**Metabolic alkalosis**: suggestive of gastric outflow or proximal duodenal obstruction; often associated with hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypochloremia

#### Antiemetic Dosages (Table 48.2)
| Drug | Site of Action | Dose |
|---|---|---|
| Prochlorperazine | CRTZ + emetic center | 0.1–0.5 mg/kg SC, IM q6–8h |
| Chlorpromazine | CRTZ + emetic center | 0.2–0.4 mg/kg SC q8h |
| Metoclopramide | CRTZ + GI smooth muscle | 0.2–0.4 mg/kg SC, IM q8h; 1–2 mg/kg/day CRI IV |
| Domperidone | CRTZ + GI smooth muscle | 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IM, IV q12h |
| Ondansetron | CRTZ + vagal afferents | 0.5–1 mg/kg PO, IV q12h |
| Dolasetron | CRTZ + vagal afferents | 0.6–1 mg/kg PO, IV q12–24h |
| **Maropitant (NK1)** | CRTZ + emetic center | 1 mg/kg SC, IV q24h; 2 mg/kg PO q24h |
| Butorphanol | CRTZ | 0.2–0.4 mg/kg IM, SC q12h |
| Diphenhydramine | CRTZ | 2–4 mg/kg PO, IM q8h |

### Ch 49 — Diarrhea
*(Author: Alison C. Manchester)*

#### Definitions
- **Diarrhea**: increased frequency, fluidity, and/or volume of bowel movements
- **Chronic diarrhea**: observed for ≥3 weeks
- Small vs large bowel differentiation:
  - **Small bowel**: ↑↑ stool volume, ↑ stool frequency, +/− weight loss, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, bloating
  - **Large bowel**: tenesmus, urgency, ↑↑ stool frequency (small volume), +/− dyschezia, mucus, fresh blood

#### Signalment/Breed Predispositions
- **EPI**: German Shepherds, Rough-Coated Collies, Cavalier King Charles Spaniels
- **Lymphangiectasia**: Yorkshire Terriers, Maltese, Chow Chows
- **Granulomatous colitis** (E. coli): Boxers, French Bulldogs
- **Protothecosis**: Rough-Coated Collies, Boxers
- **FIP**: Abyssinian, Bengal cats
- **Tritrichomoniasis**: Abyssinian, Bengal cats

#### Acute Diarrhea
- Clinically well, normal vital parameters → minimal diagnostics; bland diet, deworming, probiotics, subcutaneous fluids
- Antibiotics (metronidazole, tylosin) only when: sepsis/SIRS, neutropenia, documented non-responding enteropathogen
- Note: metronidazole causes DNA damage in feline lymphocytes → not benign in cats
- Unwell: minimum database (CBC, serum biochemistry, urinalysis, fecal parasite screen)

#### Infectious Causes of Diarrhea (Table 49.2 — selected)
| Disease | Agent | Key Features | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parvovirus/Panleukopenia | Parvovirus | Leukopenia, fever, vomiting | Fecal antigen ELISA |
| Distemper | CDV | Fever, conjunctivitis, neuro signs, nasal/footpad hyperkeratosis | Conjunctival swab PCR or DFA |
| Cryptosporidiosis | Cryptosporidium spp. | None | Fecal ELISA, DFA |
| Giardiasis | Giardia spp. | Weight loss, steatorrhea | Fecal ELISA, flotation + centrifugation, DFA |
| Salmonellosis | Salmonella spp. | Fever, abdominal pain, hematochezia | Fecal culture, PCR |
| Campylobacteriosis | Campylobacter spp. | Fever, hematochezia, cholangiohepatitis | Fecal culture, PCR |
| Hookworm | Ancylostoma, Uncinaria | Anemia, respiratory signs | Fecal flotation + centrifugation |
| Whipworm | Trichuris vulpis | Weight loss, hematochezia | Fecal flotation + centrifugation |
| Tritrichomoniasis (cats) | Tritrichomonas foetus | Hematochezia, flatulence, fecal incontinence | PCR of diarrheic feces |
| Schistosomiasis | Heterobilharzia americanum | Hypercalcemia, anemia, weight loss | Fecal PCR |
| Salmon poisoning (dogs) | Neorickettsia helminthoeca | Fever, vomiting, lymphadenopathy | Fecal sedimentation + ZnSO₄ centrifugation; blood PCR |
| Pythiosis | Pythium insidiosum | Vomiting, anorexia, abdominal mass | ELISA serologic testing |
| Histoplasmosis | Histoplasma capsulatum | Fever, anemia, respiratory/ocular signs | Urine antigen |
| Protothecosis | Prototheca spp. | Cutaneous nodules, ocular signs, vomiting | Aqueous humor cytology, urine culture |
| E. coli-GC | E. coli | Hematochezia, tenesmus, weight loss, anemia | Colonic histopathology with PAS-staining + E. coli FISH |

#### Chronic Diarrhea Workup (Fig 49.1)
1. Fecal parasite screen + deworming
2. CBC, serum biochemistry, urinalysis
3. If small bowel signs: diet trial(s); TLI, abdominal ultrasound, basal cortisol ± ACTH stim (dogs), T4 (cats)
4. If large bowel signs: fiber/diet trials; abdominal ultrasound; T4/fT4/TSH (dogs), Tritrichomonas PCR (cats)
5. Endoscopy (upper AND lower GI) + biopsy — distal esophagus to duodenum; colonoscopy separately if large bowel disease

#### Interpretation Pearls (Table 49.1)
- Lack of lymphopenia on CBC → consider hypoadrenocorticism
- Eosinophilia → hypoadrenocorticism, parasitism, neoplasia, eosinophilic enteritis, mast cell disease
- Hypoalbuminemia + low globulins → likely protein-losing enteropathy
- Hypoalbuminemia + hypocholesterolemia → consider lymphangiectasia
- BUN:creatinine ratio >30 (mg/dL; metric equivalent >0.12) → consistent with upper GI hemorrhage

### Ch 50 — Melena and Hematochezia
*(Author: Karen Michele Tefft)*

#### Definitions
- **Melena**: feces black and tarry from hematin and other hemochromes from bacterial degradation of hemoglobin; source is PROXIMAL GI (or swallowed blood from respiratory tract); ≥50–100 mL blood must be ingested before melanic stool apparent
- **Hematochezia**: bright-red colored stools; source typically cecum/colon/rectum/anus (small intestinal with increased motility also possible)
- Mimics of melena: activated charcoal, iron supplements, bismuth-containing medications, large amounts of blueberries
- Mimics of hematochezia: red food coloring, beets; perineal bite wounds; anal sac abscess

#### BUN/Creatinine Ratio
- >30 (mg/dL; metric equivalent: >0.12) consistent with upper GI hemorrhage; depends on volume of blood, time since hemorrhage, GI transit time, volemic status

#### Melena DDx (Box 50.1)

*Ingestion of Blood*
- Sinonasal lesions, pulmonary lesions, oral/pharyngeal lesions, diet (raw)

*Inflammatory*
- Esophagitis, gastroenteritis, eosinophilic gastritis, IBD

*Infectious*
- Bacterial: Campylobacter, Clostridium, Mycobacterium, Neorickettsia helminthoeca, Salmonella
- Fungal/Algal: Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, Pythium, Prototheca
- Parasitic: Spirocerca, Physaloptera, Ancylostoma, Uncinaria
- Viral: parvovirus

*Ischemic/Traumatic*
- Hypovolemic shock, thrombosis/infarction, intussusception, volvulus, foreign body, racing sled dogs

*Post-Surgical*
- Enterotomy, gastric invagination post-GDV, PEG tube placement

*Drug-Induced*
- Corticosteroids, NSAIDs, anticoagulants, platelet inhibitors, thrombolytics

*Neoplastic*
- Adenocarcinoma, GIST, leiomyoma/leiomyosarcoma, lymphoma, mast cell tumor, gastrinoma

*Vascular*
- Vascular ectasia/angiodysplasia, arteriovenous fistula (intestinal)

*Metabolic*
- Hypoadrenocorticism, uremic kidney disease, liver disease (portal hypertension/portosystemic shunt), pancreatitis, hypereosinophilic syndrome

*Bleeding Disorder*
- Thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopathia, DIC, rodenticide intoxication, specific factor deficiencies

#### Hematochezia DDx (Box 50.2)

*Unclassified*
- Acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome (AHDS)

*Inflammatory*
- IBD, histiocytic ulcerative colitis, idiopathic colitis, perianal fistulas, mucocutaneous lupus erythematosus

*Infectious*
- Bacterial: Campylobacter, Clostridium, Mycobacterium, Salmonella
- Fungal/Algal: Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, Pythium, Prototheca
- Parasitic: Ancylostoma, Uncinaria, Trichuris, coccidia, Tritrichomonas, Leishmania, Heterobilharzia americana, Entamoeba histolytica
- Viral: parvovirus

*Ischemic/Traumatic*
- Hypovolemic shock, thrombosis/infarction, intussusception, cecal inversion, volvulus, foreign body, pelvic fracture, rectoanal stricture, racing sled dogs

*Drug-Induced*
- Corticosteroids, NSAIDs, anticoagulants, platelet inhibitors, thrombolytics, cytotoxic chemotherapy drugs

*Neoplastic*
- Adenocarcinoma, GIST, leiomyoma/leiomyosarcoma, lymphoma, plasmacytoma, colorectal polyp

*Vascular*
- Vascular ectasia/angiodysplasia

*Metabolic*
- Hypoadrenocorticism, uremic kidney disease, liver disease (portal hypertension/portosystemic shunts), pancreatitis

*Bleeding Disorder*
- Thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopathia, DIC, rodenticide intoxication, specific factor deficiencies

#### Red Flag: "Raspberry Jam" Hematochezia
- Severe acute hemorrhagic diarrhea syndrome (AHDS); red-maroon feces throughout suggest proximal colonic lesion; surface blood only → anorectal lesion

### Ch 51 — Constipation, Tenesmus, Dyschezia, and Fecal Incontinence
*(Author: Emily N. Gould)*

#### Definitions
- **Constipation**: reduced frequency or absence of defecation; retention of hard, dry feces; total fecal volume often decreased
- **Obstipation**: inability to defecate without medical intervention; result of prolonged constipation; not all constipated animals become obstipated
- **Tenesmus**: repeated nonproductive straining to defecate or urinate; usually accompanied by LI disease signs (hematochezia, mucus, increased frequency/reduced volume); precedes defecation in obstructive disease; follows defecation in inflammatory disease
- **Dyschezia**: painful defecation; typically anorectal rather than colonic etiology
- **Fecal incontinence**: failure to retain feces; involuntary "leakage"

#### DDx — Constipation
**Mechanical**
- Low-insoluble-fiber diet → decreased colonic motility
- Pica (bones, hair, wool, cat litter, plant material)
- Congenital: sacral spinal cord abnormalities (Manx cats, some brachycephalic dogs); atresia ani (Poodles, Boston Terriers)
- Lumbar/sacral/pelvic canal trauma
- Severe prostatomegaly (extraluminal obstruction)
- Idiopathic: feline idiopathic megacolon (recurrent constipation → obstipation)

**Metabolic/Nutritional**
- Hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia
- Prolonged dehydration
- PU/PD diseases (CKD, diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism)
- Obesity; prolonged inactivity

**Neurologic/Endocrine**
- Dysautonomia (rare; more often cats, also dogs)
- Hypothyroidism (cats: especially congenital kittens)

#### DDx — Tenesmus and Dyschezia
**Intraluminal obstruction**: neoplasia, FB, strictures
**Extraluminal obstruction**: compressive abdominal mass/organomegaly, pelvic fractures, pseudocoprostasis
**Infectious**: Trichuris, Ancylostoma spp.; Tritrichomonas foetus (cats; tenesmus, dyschezia, foul-smelling LI diarrhea); Pythium, Histoplasma, Prototheca (can cause marked colonic disease)
**Inflammatory**: CIE, fiber-responsive LBD (FRLBD), food-responsive enteropathies (FRE), stress colitis (dogs)
**Structural**: perianal fistulas (GSDs overrepresented), anal sacculitis, perineal hernia
**Congenital**: atresia ani (Poodles, Boston Terriers)

#### DDx — Fecal Incontinence
**Neurogenic**
- UMN sphincter incompetence: focal (arachnoid cysts, IVDD, masses) or diffuse (inflammatory CNS disorders, dysautonomia)
- IVDD; degenerative myelopathy (DM in GSDs, Pembroke Welsh Corgis); sacrocaudal luxations ("tail-pull"); discospondylitis; cauda equina syndrome
- Diffuse LMN disease

**Non-neurogenic**
- Reservoir incontinence: severe colon/rectum inflammation; subtotal colectomy
- External sphincter incompetence: aging, behavioral disorders, trauma, neoplasia
- Intoxications (vincristine, macadamia nuts) → transient peripheral neuropathies

> ClinIQ: no matching sign screen (candidate — Constipation/Tenesmus)

### Ch 52 — Flatulence
*(Author: Genevieve Mak)*

#### Definitions and Physiology
- Flatulence: gas expelled through anus; dogs/cats normally pass flatus multiple times daily
- >99% of GI gas = odorless (CO₂, H₂, methane, nitrogen, oxygen); <1% sulfur-based (odiferous)
- ~75% of flatus = H₂, methane, CO₂ (from bacterial fermentation)
- Brachycephalic breeds: aerophagia → increased gas production → higher frequency and more odorous feces

#### Differential Diagnosis
**Primary causes of excessive flatulence**
- High-FODMAP diet (oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, polyols): wheat, rye, leeks, zucchini, dairy (lactose), fruits (apples, pears, peaches, mangoes, apricots), lentils, legumes, cabbage, brussels sprouts, green beans
- Any primary GI disease that impairs fermentation/absorption: EPI (when associated with malabsorption), IBD, diarrhea
- Aerophagia: brachycephalic breeds, excited or stressed animals
- High protein/fermentable-fiber diets

**"Emergency treatment"**: open windows

#### Management (Fig 52.1)
1. Diet change (avoid FODMAPs); trial each diet 6–8 weeks
2. Probiotics (conflicting evidence; may reduce flatulence/bloating in some)
3. Prebiotics: modulate microbiota; beneficial fecal metabolite shifts
4. Yucca schidigera extract: improves fecal odor (binds ammonia); does not reduce total gas or frequency
5. Activated charcoal: binds sulfur gases (reduces odor, not gas production)
6. Simethicone: anti-foaming agent; theoretical reduction in bloating; dose 20–200 mg/dog PO up to q6h; no studies in dogs/cats
7. Antibiotics: NOT recommended for flatulence alone (promotes resistance); only if concurrent SIBO/IBD

> ClinIQ: no matching sign screen (candidate — Flatulence)

### Ch 53 — Polyuria and Polydipsia
*(Author: Robert E. Shiel)*

#### Definitions/Thresholds
- **Polydipsia (PD)**: water intake >90–100 mL/kg/day (dogs); >50 mL/kg/day (cats)
- **Polyuria (PU)**: urine output >50 mL/kg/day (both species)
- USG in health: 1.006–1.050 (dogs); 1.005–1.090 (cats)
- Results consistently >1.030 (dogs) or >1.035 (cats) = strong evidence against PU unless glycosuria or intermittent PU
- **Marked hyposthenuria** (USG <1.006) in dogs: most commonly hyperadrenocorticism, CDI, hypercalcemia, hypoadrenocorticism, liver disease, or primary polydipsia

#### Serum Osmolality Formula (conventional units)
`Serum Osmolality (mOsm/kg) = 2[Na⁺] + [glucose/18] + [BUN/2.8]`

#### USG interpretation note
- USG increases ~0.004 per g/dL glucose (may vary up to 0.008 in dilute urine with 2.4 g/dL/133 mmol/L glucose added)

#### Full DDx — Box 53.1: Causes of PU/PD

**Central Diabetes Insipidus (CDI)**
- Neoplasia, inflammation, trauma, developmental defects, idiopathic
- Complete or partial AVP deficiency

**Primary Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus (NDI)**
- Rare hereditary disorder; severe PU/PD at early age
- Dogs only (*not reported in cats)

**Secondary Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus**
- Hyperadrenocorticism
- Hypercalcemia
- Hypoadrenocorticism
- Liver disease
- Hyperthyroidism
- Pyometra/E. coli endotoxemia
- Pyelonephritis
- Hypokalemia
- Erythrocytosis* (dogs only)
- Hyperaldosteronism
- Hypersomatotropism (acromegaly)
- Leptospirosis* (dogs; rare as isolated PU cause)
- Drug administration: glucocorticoids, phenobarbital

**Disturbed Osmotic Gradient (osmotic diuresis)**
- Diabetes mellitus
- Fanconi syndrome* (dogs)
- Primary renal glycosuria* (dogs)
- Post-obstructive diuresis
- Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
- Syndrome of inappropriate diuresis (SIAD)*
- High-salt or -protein diet
- Drug administration: mannitol
- Decreased medullary tonicity: renal medullary washout; low-protein or -salt diet

**Other/Unknown Mechanisms**
- Polyuric phase of acute kidney injury
- Pheochromocytoma
- Splenic hemangiosarcoma* (dogs only)
- Intestinal leiomyosarcoma* (dogs only)
- Primary polydipsia (PP; psychogenic)

*Described as cause of PU/PD in dogs but not cats

#### Cats-Specific Note
- PU/PD most common in CKD, diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism, CDI
- Primary NDI not reported in cats; one possible PP case in literature
- Outdoor cats/multi-cat households: difficult to measure water intake and urine output
- Cats may be resistant to PU due to greater urine concentrating ability and tolerance to dehydration

#### Diagnostic Approach (Fig 53.1)
**Step 1**: Confirm PU/PD with measured water intake at home; multiple urine samples over several days
**Step 2**: Signalment, history, PE (age, breed, sex, neuter status, medications)
**Step 3**: CBC, serum biochemistry, urinalysis (± electrolytes); glycosuria confirms DM or renal tubular disease (exclude stress hyperglycemia in cats); isosthenuria/hyposthenuria = renal azotemia; concentrated urine = pre-renal azotemia; hyposthenuria in pre-renal pattern = hypoadrenocorticism
**Step 4**: Additional testing based on clinical suspicion
- Urine culture: for pyelonephritis (challenging to exclude)
- Abdominal ultrasonography: adrenal, liver, kidney diseases; pyometra; splenic hemangiosarcoma; intestinal leiomyosarcoma
- Specific tests: liver function, hyperadrenocorticism (LDDS/HDDS/ACTH stim), hyperthyroidism (T4), acromegaly (IGF-1)
- SDMA or GFR: for early/preclinical CKD
- MRI: if brain disease suspected (CDI)

**Step 5**: Modified water deprivation test or desmopressin trial (ONLY after all other DDx excluded)
- Modified water deprivation test: distinguishes PP vs CDI vs primary NDI; risk of severe hypertonic dehydration (potentially fatal)
- Desmopressin trial: alternative to water deprivation test (especially in cats)

> ClinIQ: maps to PU/PD

### Ch 54 — Pollakiuria, Stranguria, and Urinary Incontinence
*(Author: Mary Anna Labato)*

#### Definitions
- **Urinary incontinence**: involuntary escape of urine during storage phase; most common = intermittent or continuous dribbling + episodes of normal voiding
- **Detrusor hyperspasticity/instability**: spontaneous uninhibited detrusor contractions (overactive bladder); frequent voiding of small volumes; often underlying cystitis; cats: FIC/Pandora syndrome
- **Pollakiuria**: abnormally frequent passage of small amounts of urine
- **Stranguria**: slow, painful discharge of urine from urethral/bladder spasms; urine passed drop by drop with pain and even tenesmus
- **Dysuria**: difficult or painful urination; "catch-all" term for stranguria or pollakiuria
- Residual urine volume: should not exceed 0.4 mL/kg in normal animals

#### Causes of Pollakiuria (Box 54.1)
- Infection: bacterial, mycoplasmal, viral, fungal, parasitic (bladder, prostate)
- Inflammation: polypoid cystitis, pyogranulomatous cystitis, granulomatous urethritis, follicular vaginitis
- Urocystolithiasis
- Neoplasia: transitional cell carcinoma, prostatic adenocarcinoma, vaginal leiomyoma/sarcoma
- Detrusor atony (partial obstruction)
- Urethral stricture
- Feline idiopathic cystitis (FIC)/Pandora syndrome
- Chemical/drugs (e.g., cyclophosphamide)
- Anatomic abnormalities: perineal hernia with retroflexed bladder, spay granuloma, uterine stump disease
- Iatrogenic: urethral irritation from catheterization, palpation, voiding urohydropropulsion, overdistension from flushing

#### Causes of Stranguria (Box 54.2)
- Cystitis: infectious vs sterile inflammatory
- Urethritis: infectious vs sterile inflammatory
- Urocystolithiasis
- Vaginitis: follicular (inflammatory) vs infectious
- Neoplasia: urethral TCC, prostatic adenocarcinoma, vaginal leiomyoma/sarcoma
- Prostatic disease: prostatitis, prostatic abscess, neoplasia
- Trauma, foreign body
- FIC/Pandora syndrome
- Ruptured bladder
- Urethral stricture

#### Causes of Urge Incontinence (Box 54.3)
- Detrusor hyperspasticity (idiopathic)
- Cystitis/urethritis: infectious vs sterile inflammatory
- Anatomical abnormality: ectopic ureter(s)
- Pelvic bladder, urethral dysplasia
- Neurological abnormality: UMN bladder
- Urethral sphincter mechanism incompetence
- Urethral stricture

#### Neurological Examination in Incontinence
- LMN bladder: reduced sphincter tone, easy manual expression
- UMN bladder: increased sphincter tone, difficult manual expression
- Perineal reflex: evaluates pudendal nerve
- Bulbospongiosus reflex: pudendal nerve + sacral spinal segments

#### Key Distinction: FIC in Cats
- FIC: self-limiting; most common age 1–6 years; equal males and females; male cats risk urethral obstruction (life-threatening emergency)
- Older cats: bacterial UTI more likely; also stones (struvite, calcium oxalate)

> ClinIQ: no matching sign screen (candidate — Pollakiuria/Stranguria/Urinary Incontinence)

### Ch 55 — Hematuria and Other Conditions Causing Discolored Urine
*(Author: [not named in extracted pages — Bartges JW cited from 7th ed])*

#### Definitions
- **Hematuria**: red blood cells in urine; turbid red-brown on visual inspection; clear supernatant on centrifugation
- **Hemoglobinuria**: transparent red/brown; no RBCs on sediment; pink plasma if hemoglobinemia present → suggests intravascular hemolysis; haptoglobin binding capacity exceeded
- **Myoglobinuria**: clear plasma (myoglobin not protein-bound; rapidly cleared); no RBCs on sediment; serum CK markedly elevated → severe muscle damage, thrombosis

#### Urine Color Diagnostic Approach (Table 55.1 + Fig 55.2)

**Red/Pink/Brown/Orange or Red-Brown urine:**
1. Test strip positive for blood?
   - Yes → urine sediment: RBCs present? → Hematuria
   - Yes → no RBCs → check plasma color → pink = hemoglobinuria; colorless → check CK/AST → elevated = myoglobinuria
   - No → suspect bilirubinuria → urine dipstick bilirubin + serum bilirubin → if negative → other pigments (drugs, dyes; Table 55.1)

**Colorless urine**: very dilute (diuretics, DI, glucocorticoid excess, fluid therapy, overhydration)

**Yellow-brown or green-brown**: bile pigments

**Brown/Black**: methemoglobinuria, copper toxicosis, fecal contamination; melanin

**Milky white**: lipiduria, pyuria (most common: bacterial UTI), crystalluria

#### Hematuria Causes (Fig 55.2)
- Bleeding disorder
- Urolithiasis
- Urinary tract infection
- Neoplasia
- Trauma
- Benign renal hematuria

#### Minimum Workup for Hematuria
- History, CBC, coagulation profile, urine culture, diagnostic imaging, uroendoscopy

> ClinIQ: maps to Haematuria

### Ch 56 — Vulvar and Preputial Discharge
*(Author: Jeffrey de Gier)*

#### Overview
- Physiological vaginal discharges (not worrisome): bitches during proestrus, pregnancy, parturition, days-to-weeks post-parturition; queens during/after parturition
- Physiological preputial discharge in males: mucopurulent without clinical signs = normal/inconsequential
- Invasive vaginal examination usually not feasible in awake cats or prepubertal bitches

#### Serosanguineous Vaginal Discharge — Intact Bitches/Queens (Fig 56.2)

**With estrogen influence (confirmed by vaginal cytology, vaginoscopy)**
- Physiological: proestrus
- Prolonged duration:
  - Ovarian neoplasia
  - Cystic ovarian follicles
  - Failure to ovulate ("split heats") — persistent low plasma progesterone
  - Exogenous estrogen
  - Portosystemic shunt
  - Pituitary hypofunction

**Without estrogen influence**
- Endometritis (most common pathological cause after estrus or parturition)
- Neoplasia of urogenital tract (often benign: leiomyoma, fibroma; evaluate by cytology/histopathology)
- Subinvolution of placental sites (SIPS): prolonged bloody discharge >2–3 weeks post-parturition in otherwise healthy bitches; smear shows erythrocytes, occasional neutrophils, vacuolated giant cells; resolves at next estrus
- Rarely: trauma, hemorrhagic diathesis, foreign body (vagina)
- In queens: endometritis or (partial) abortion → bloody discharge; rarely trauma, diathesis, foreign body

#### Serosanguineous After Ovariectomy/OVH

**With estrogen influence**
- Remnant ovarian tissue (ROT): confirmed by plasma progesterone >2 ng/mL; GnRH stimulation test or AMH to confirm; basal LH alone not reliable
- Exogenous estrogen administration

**Without estrogen influence**
- Stump endometritis: only possible with ROT (progesterone influence) or progestins
- Uterine stump hemorrhage (1–2 weeks post-OVH)
- Neoplasia of urogenital tract (more often malignant than in intact bitches)
- Rarely: trauma, hemorrhagic diathesis, foreign body

#### Mucopurulent Vaginal Discharge — Intact (Fig 56.7)

**Physiological**
- Onset of diestrus (several days)
- Pregnancy (~day 30: clear mucus)

**Pathological**
- Endometritis (post-estrum, post-partum)
- Abortion (often dark green discharge)
- Vestibulitis/vaginitis (primary or secondary):
  - Primary vaginitis: prepubertal (puppy vaginitis) — NOT seen in cats; or after 1st/2nd estrus (especially large/brachycephalic breeds; often self-limiting after 1st estrus); treatment with antibiotics not recommended pre-1st estrus
  - Secondary vaginitis: various causes
  - Infrequently: canine herpesvirus infection (vestibule)
- Neoplasia (usually benign)
- Foreign body (vagina)

**"Puppy Vaginitis"**
- Prepubertal large/brachycephalic breeds (as early as 3 months)
- Slightly swollen vulva, mucoid white/yellow discharge, attraction of males
- Self-limiting; disappears after 1st estrous cycle or after 2nd–3rd luteal phases
- Treatment pre-1st estrus NOT recommended; antibiotics do not help

**After OVH (mucopurulent)**
- Vaginitis (usually secondary)
- Stump endometritis (requires ROT + progesterone influence or exogenous progestins)
- Hypersecretion of vaginal mucosa (if continuing estrogen influence, e.g., ROT)
- Rarely: neoplasia (lower prevalence; more often malignant), foreign body

#### Preputial Discharge (Fig 56.14)

**Mucopurulent**
- Balanoposthitis
- Prostatitis
- Penile neoplasia
- Foreign body

**Serosanguineous**
- Benign prostatic hyperplasia
- Balanoposthitis
- Prostatitis
- Urethral prolapse
- Penile/urethral: trauma, calculus, neoplasia
- Hemorrhagic diathesis
- Foreign body

> ClinIQ: no matching sign screen (candidate — Vulvar/Preputial Discharge)

## Section III — Differential Diagnosis for Clinicopathologic Abnormalities
### Ettinger's Textbook of Veterinary Internal Medicine, 9th edition (Chapters 57–71)

---

### Ch 57 — Anemia and Erythrocytosis

#### Reference Thresholds / Definitions
- **Anemia**: PCV/HCT/HB/RBC below the lower reference limit for the species.
- **Erythrocytosis**: PCV/HCT/HB/RBC above the upper reference limit.
- **PCV vs HCT distinction**: PCV is direct (microhematocrit); HCT is calculated (MCV × RBC). Median PCV–HCT difference = −0.02 L/L (dog) and −0.03 L/L (cat).
- **Breed caution (dog)**: Greyhounds normally have higher HCTs — a result of 0.45 L/L (45%) may indicate anemia in this breed despite being within standard reference intervals.
- **Regenerative response timing**: Bone marrow takes ~3–5 days to mount a regenerative response; do not classify as non-regenerative before this window.

#### Reticulocyte Interpretation
- **Moderate to marked polychromasia** (>7 RBCs per 100× oil immersion field): likely regenerative regardless of severity.
- **Mild polychromasia** (<3 RBCs per 100× field): "adequate" regeneration difficult to assess.
- **Absolute reticulocyte count** (above upper reference limit for the lab) = most reliable marker of adequacy.
- Example regenerative case: dog with 0.25 L/L HCT (RI 0.41–0.58) → reticulocytes 10%, absolute 348 × 10⁹/L (RI 11–92 × 10⁹/L).
- Cats: only aggregate reticulocytes are counted; punctate reticulocytes are not included.

#### 4-Step Mechanistic Approach to Anemia
1. **How acute is the anemia?** (Pre-regenerative if <3–5 days old)
2. **Is the anemia regenerative?** (Use absolute reticulocyte count ± polychromasia)
3. **Is a cause identifiable on blood smear?**
4. **Which additional tests are indicated?**

#### DDx for Regenerative Anemia (Hemorrhage vs Hemolysis)
| Mechanism | Key features |
|---|---|
| **Hemorrhage** | Low total protein (esp. albumin + globulins); iron deficiency if chronic external loss (hypochromic microcytic RBCs, low iron/transferrin saturation) |
| **Hemolysis — extravascular** | Normal/high total protein; high bilirubin (unconjugated); high iron/transferrin saturation; siderocytes |
| **Hemolysis — intravascular component** | As above plus hemoglobinemia + hemoglobinuria; ghost RBCs on smear |

**Blood smear clues for hemolysis mechanism:**
- Spherocytes (moderate to many): IMHA
- Heinz bodies + eccentrocytes: oxidant injury (zinc, onions [dog], acetaminophen [cat], skunk musk)
- Acanthocytes + schistocytes + keratocytes: fragmentation (DIC, vasculitis)
- Organisms on smear: Babesia spp., Mycoplasma haemofelis (cats), M. haemocanis (dogs; uncommon cause of anemia)

#### DDx — Hemolysis (by cause)
- **Immune-mediated (IMHA)**: Primary (autoimmune) or associative (secondary to infection, drugs, blood-group incompatibility). Common in dogs; uncommon in cats.
- **Infectious**: Babesia sp., Theileria sp., Mycoplasma haemocanis/haemofelis; only M. haemofelis is a common cause of hemolytic anemia in cats.
- **Oxidant-induced**: Zinc (dogs), onion/garlic (dogs and cats), acetaminophen (cats), skunk musk (dogs).
- **Fragmentation (microangiopathic)**: Vasculitis, DIC. Often non-regenerative due to concurrent anemia of inflammatory disease.
- **Aberrant macrophage activity**: Hemophagocytic histiocytic sarcoma.
- **Inherited RBC defects**: Phosphofructokinase deficiency (dog), pyruvate kinase deficiency (dogs and cats), stomatocytosis (Alaskan Malamute), spherocytosis (Golden Retriever).
- **Miscellaneous**: Severe hypophosphatemia, envenomation (snakes, bees).

#### DDx — Non-Regenerative Anemia

| Index type | Consider |
|---|---|
| Macrocytic normochromic | FeLV (cats); rule out breed-associated (Miniature/Toy Poodles) |
| Normocytic normochromic (mild–moderate) | Anemia of inflammatory disease; anemia of chronic kidney disease; endocrine disease (hypothyroidism, hypoadrenocorticism); cancer-associated anemia |
| Normocytic normochromic (severe) | Immune-mediated (precursor-directed IMHA); FeLV; acute leukemia; bone marrow aplasia |
| Microcytic hypochromic | Iron deficiency (chronic blood loss); functional iron deficiency (portosystemic shunts); rule out breed-associated (Shar-Pei, Siberian Husky) |

**Other non-regenerative causes:**
- **Bone marrow disease**: Ineffective erythropoiesis (immune-mediated, drugs/estrogen, toxins, Ehrlichia canis, histiocytic sarcoma); myelodysplastic syndrome; leukemia; myelofibrosis; parvovirus (destruction of erythroid progenitors); recombinant human EPO antibodies.
- **Decreased HB production**: Iron deficiency; lead toxicosis (chronic).
- **Decreased DNA synthesis**: Vitamin B12/folate deficiency (rare); FeLV infection.
- Bone marrow aspiration indicated for: pancytopenia; severe non-regenerative anemia without another cause; suspected leukemia or neoplastic infiltration.

#### Erythrocytosis
**Relative (not true) increase**: Dehydration (high total protein); splenic contraction (transient, epinephrine).

**Absolute (true) erythrocytosis:**
- **Appropriate secondary**: Hypoxia → EPO release (cardiac disease, right-to-left shunting PDA, respiratory disease).
- **Inappropriate secondary**: Non-hypoxic EPO release — most often renal disease (neoplastic: renal carcinoma, T-cell lymphoma; non-neoplastic: pyelonephritis); other paraneoplastic (cecal leiomyosarcoma).
- **Primary (polycythemia vera)**: Rare; JAK2 mutation documented in dogs; diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out secondary causes.

**Algorithm**: Increased HCT → Rule out high total protein/dehydration → If persistent: measure pO₂ → If no hypoxia: assess kidneys → If no renal lesion: assess for other neoplasia → If none: consider polycythemia vera (confirm JAK2 mutation or by exclusion).

(Ch 57)

---

### Ch 58 — Leukopenia, Leukocytosis

#### Key Thresholds
- **Neutropenia thresholds** (dog and cat):
  - Mild: 1,500–3,000 cells/mcL
  - Moderate: 500–1,500 cells/mcL
  - Severe: <500 cells/mcL — risk of fever and opportunistic infection; treat emergently if febrile
- **Severe leukocytosis threshold**: >35,000 cells/mcL (previously called "leukemoid response")
- **Degenerative left shift** prognostic: hazard ratio for death/euthanasia = 1.9 in dogs; 1.75 in cats

#### Causes of Severe Neutrophilic Leukocytosis (WBC >50,000/mcL)
| Category | Dogs (Lucroy) | Dogs (Weltan) | Cats (Lucroy) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Infection | 34% (40/115) | 58%* (106/182) | 37% (38/104) |
| Immune-mediated | 32% (38/115) | 11% | 22% |
| Neoplasia | 20% (24/115) | 14% | 23% |
| Tissue necrosis | 10% (12/115) | 13% | 18% |
*Includes Babesiosis group (50/182).

**Other causes of severe neutrophilic leukocytosis**: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency; paraneoplastic leukocytosis; Babesia infection; Hepatozoon canis; IMHA; bacterial prostatitis.

**Physiologic neutrophilia limit**: Should not exceed 2× upper reference limit and should not produce a left shift.

#### Toxic Neutrophil Changes
(Indicate accelerated maturation; raise suspicion for infection)
- Cytoplasmic basophilia
- Döhle bodies
- Increased vacuolization
- Decreased nuclear condensation
- Increased granules

**Causes of Neutropenia** (dogs/cats, Brown et al., n=261):
| Category | % |
|---|---|
| Infectious disease | 52%* |
| Increased demand | 11% |
| Drug-induced | 11% |
| Primary bone marrow disease | 4% |
*123/124 dogs: parvovirus; 10/11 cats: FeLV or FIV.

**Drug causes of neutropenia**: Chloramphenicol, azathioprine, phenobarbital, phenylbutazone, methimazole, sulfa derivatives, chemotherapy agents.

#### Differential Diagnosis Summary (E-Figure 58.2)

**Neutrophilia:**
- Glucocorticoid-associated: stress, hyperadrenocorticism, glucocorticoid therapy, ACTH administration
- Catecholamine-associated: fight-or-flight, catecholamine administration
- Inflammatory: bacterial/fungal/protozoal/viral/parasitic infections; necrosis (hemolysis, ischemia, thermal, neoplasia); sterile inflammation (pancreatitis, FIP, immune-mediated)
- Neoplastic: granulocytic leukemia; paraneoplastic
- Other: regenerative anemia; leukocyte adhesion deficiency; G-CSF/GM-CSF administration; early estrogen toxicosis

**Lymphocytosis:**
- Catecholamine-associated (fight-or-flight)
- Chronic antigenic stimulation (bacterial, rickettsial, fungal, viral, protozoal especially Babesia)
- Other: hypoadrenocorticism, recent vaccination, lymphoplasmacytic enteritis/hepatitis
- Neoplastic: lymphoma with leukemic phase; lymphoid leukemia
- Note: cats more likely than dogs to develop reactive lymphocytosis with inflammation; usually mild but can be 2–3× upper reference limit

**Eosinophilia:** Hypersensitivity; parasitism (ectoparasites, heartworms, tissue nematodes); mast cell disorder; fungal infections; hypereosinophilic syndrome; eosinophilic myositis/gastroenteritis/panosteitis; paraneoplastic; eosinophilic leukemia; mast cell tumors; lymphoma.

**Basophilia:** Hypersensitivity; parasitism; drugs; insect envenomation; inflammation; paraneoplastic; mast cell tumor; basophilic leukemia; feline myeloproliferative disease; essential thrombocythemia; polycythemia vera.

**Monocytosis:** Inflammatory (infections, necrosis, sterile inflammation); glucocorticoid-associated; monocytic/myelomonocytic leukemia; immune-mediated neutropenia; cyclic hematopoiesis; GM-CSF administration.

**Neutropenia:** Cyclic hematopoiesis (Gray Collie); bone marrow disorder (necrosis, infection, drug reaction, toxicosis, chemotherapy, radiation, immune-mediated, myelophthisis, myelodysplasia, neoplasia, nutrient deficiency, trapped neutrophil syndrome); overwhelming inflammation.

**Lymphopenia:** Glucocorticoid-associated (stress, hyperadrenocorticism, therapy); lymphoid hypoplasia/aplasia (irradiation, immunosuppressive drugs, multicentric lymphoma); depletion (chylothorax, protein-losing enteropathy, lymphangiectasia); acute inflammation (bacterial/viral infection, endotoxemia).

#### Chronic Idiopathic Neutropenia in Cats
- Mild to moderate; counts occasionally <1,000/mcL; no left shift, toxic changes, clinical signs, or recurrent infection.
- Diagnosis by exclusion after ruling out retroviral infections; bone marrow assessment not needed.

(Ch 58)

---

### Ch 59 — Thrombocytopenia, Thrombocytosis

#### Reference Intervals (Cornell, Advia 2120)
| Species | Platelet count (× 10³/mcL) | Mean Platelet Volume (fL) |
|---|---|---|
| Canine | 186–545 | 8.4–14.1 |
| Feline | 195–624 | 9.1–24.3 |

#### Clinical Bleeding Threshold
- Spontaneous hemorrhage rarely the **sole** cause at platelet count >30,000/mcL.
- Primary ITP: typically platelet count <50,000/mcL at diagnosis.
- Severe thrombocytopenia (immune-mediated destruction): often <20,000/mcL.

#### Smear Estimation Formula
Platelet count (per mcL) = average platelets/field (10 oil-immersion fields) × 15,000

#### Classification of Thrombocytopenia (Figure 59.1)

**1. Production Defects** (high MPV, high % reticulated platelets indicate newly released):
- **Infiltrative disorders**: Leukemia (ALL, AML, CLL), non-leukemic neoplasia (lymphoma, myeloma, mast cells, histiocytes, metastatic carcinoma), myelodysplasia, myelofibrosis.
- **Drug toxicosis**: See Box 59.1 (antibiotics: cephalosporins, chloramphenicol, griseofulvin, penicillins, sulfonamides; anti-inflammatories: acetaminophen, carprofen, ibuprofen, phenylbutazone; cardiac/respiratory: procainamide, quinidine, thiazide diuretics; cytotoxic: azathioprine, chlorambucil, cisplatin, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin; miscellaneous: estrogens, phenobarbital, propylthiouracil, methimazole).
- **Infectious**: See Box 59.2.
- **Endocrine**: Estrogen toxicosis (functional ovarian granulosa cell tumor, Sertoli cell tumor, exogenous estrogen); hypothyroidism (rarely causes clinically relevant thrombocytopenia).
- **Hereditary defects**:
  - Greyhounds: mild subclinical reduction.
  - Cavalier King Charles Spaniels: macrothrombocytopenia, platelet count 25,000–75,000/mcL; beta1-tubulin gene mutation. Same mutation also in Chihuahuas, Labrador Retrievers, Shih Tzus.
  - Norfolk/Cairn Terriers: distinct beta1-tubulin mutation.
  - Cats: felid-specific beta1-tubulin structural variant causes wide variation in platelet size/count; does not cause bleeding tendency.

**2. Destruction and Consumption Defects:**
- **Primary ITP**: Middle-aged dogs, females over-represented; Cocker Spaniels, Poodles, Old English Sheepdogs predisposed. Cats less commonly affected. Diagnosis: exclusion of underlying disease + severe thrombocytopenia (<50,000/mcL) + normal to increased megakaryopoiesis + response to immunosuppressives.
- **Secondary immune thrombocytopenia**: Associated with infection, neoplasia, drug exposure, transfusion.
- **Activation/consumption**: DIC; infectious/non-infectious vasculitides.
- **Sequestration (hypersplenism)**: Neoplasia (mast cell, lymphoma, hemangiosarcoma), inflammation, congestive portal hypertension/heart failure.

**Pathogens causing infectious thrombocytopenia (Box 59.2):**
- Viral (feline): FeLV, FIV, panleukopenia virus, FIPV
- Viral (canine): distemper, herpesvirus, parvovirus, adenovirus
- Parasitic/arthropod-borne: Anaplasma (platys, phagocytophilum), Angiostrongylus, Babesia, Bartonella, Borrelia, Cytauxzoon felis, Dirofilaria, Ehrlichia (canis, platys, ewingii), Leishmania, Mycoplasma haemofelis, Rickettsia rickettsii
- Fungal/bacterial: Gram-negative/positive bacteria (septicemia), Candida, Histoplasma, Leptospira spp.

**3. Dilutional Defects**: Massive transfusion (>1 blood volume in 1 day) or high-volume resuscitation (>50% blood volume in 4 hours).

#### Thrombocytosis

**Primary (Essential) Thrombocythemia**: Autonomous; marked platelet elevation **>900,000/mcL**; rare myeloproliferative disease; JAK2, CALR, MPL driver mutations. Signs: fever, splenomegaly, anemia, thrombosis, hemorrhage.

**Reactive (Secondary) Thrombocytosis**: Chronic blood loss, infection, inflammation, malignancy, tissue necrosis; mediated by TPO and other cytokines. No specific signs; resolves with treatment of underlying disorder.

(Ch 59)

---

### Ch 60 — Hypoproteinemia and Hyperproteinemia

#### Albumin: Key Concepts
- ~80% of colloid oncotic pressure; synthesized by liver; requires >80% hepatocyte loss for decreased production.
- **Albumin thresholds**:
  - Mildly low: 2.1–2.5 g/dL (21–25 g/L)
  - Moderately low: 1.5–2.0 g/dL (15–20 g/L)
  - Severely low: <1.5 g/dL (<15 g/L) → risk of effusions, edema, thromboembolic complications (concurrent AT loss)
- Serum albumin >1.5–2 mg/dL usually does not result in significant effusion unless concurrent portal hypertension.
- Fluid protein >2.5–3 g/dL (>25–30 g/L) in an effusion: consistent with exudative process.

#### Algorithm: Hypoalbuminemia (Figure 60.1)
**Low albumin + Normal globulins → Decreased production or specific protein-losing conditions:**
- Hepatic dysfunction/PSS → serum bile acids, ammonia, CT/angiogram, liver biopsy
- Hypoadrenocorticism → baseline cortisol; if <2.0 mcg/dL (<55 nmol/L) → ACTH stimulation test
- PLN → urinalysis/UPC; if UPC >2.0 → renal biopsy
- Critical illness / acute-phase reaction

**Low albumin + Low globulins → GI loss most likely:**
- PLE → fecal alpha-1-protease inhibitor; GI biopsies
- Also: vasculitis/sepsis ("third-spacing")

**Rule-out thresholds:**
- PLN: UPC <2.0 rules out significant proteinuria
- Hypoadrenocorticism: baseline cortisol >2 mcg/dL (>55 nmol/L) = unlikely

#### Hyperglobulinemia
- Serum globulins >5.0 mg/dL (50 g/L): consider SPE
- **Polyclonal gammopathy** (broad beta–gamma peak): Chronic antigenic stimulation, acute-phase proteins, inflammatory/infectious/immune-mediated/neoplastic processes.
- **Monoclonal gammopathy** (narrow "spike" in beta or gamma): Neoplastic (multiple myeloma, extramedullary plasma cell tumor, lymphoma, CLL, Waldenström macroglobulinemia) or non-neoplastic (heartworm, ehrlichiosis, leishmaniasis, FIP, bartonellosis).
- **Hyperviscosity syndrome**: Globulins >6 g/dL (>60 g/L), particularly IgM, IgA, IgG → epistaxis, gum bleeding, retinal hemorrhage, hyphema, neurological signs.

(Ch 60)

---

### Ch 61 — Hypoglycemia and Hyperglycemia

#### Sample Handling Pearls
- Gold standard: serum or plasma separated promptly OR fluoride oxalate / citrate buffer tubes (prevent in vitro glycolysis).
- Storage without centrifugation at room temperature: significant BG decrease within 1–2 hours (lithium heparin and serum samples lose ~15–20% by 4h).
- Human PBGMs underestimate BG in dogs and cats; always confirm with reference laboratory analyzer.
- Severe polycythemia or leukocytosis can cause in vitro hypoglycemia.
- Anemia can cause falsely **increased** BG (may mask hypoglycemia).

#### Renal Glucosuria Thresholds
- Dogs: glucosuria when blood glucose >170–180 mg/dL (>9.4–10 mmol/L)
- Cats: glucosuria when blood glucose >260–310 mg/dL (>14.4–17.2 mmol/L)

#### ALIVE* Criteria for Diabetes Mellitus Diagnosis

**Dogs:**
1. Random BG ≥200 mg/dL (≥11 mmol/L) with classic signs (PU/PD, polyphagia, weight loss) or hyperglycemic crisis; OR
2. Fasting BG >125 mg/dL to ≤200 mg/dL (>7 to ≤11 mmol/L) with persistent fasting hyperglycemia >24h OR increased glycated proteins.

**Cats (stress hyperglycemia warrants caution):**
1. Random BG ≥270 mg/dL (≥15 mmol/L) with classic signs (with no other plausible cause) or hyperglycemic crisis AND at least one of: increased glycated protein OR glucosuria on ≥2 naturally voided samples at home ≥2 days after stressful event; OR
2. Random BG >125 to ≤270 mg/dL (>7 to ≤15 mmol/L) with at least two of: classic clinical signs, increased glycated protein, glucosuria (as above).

#### Potential Causes of Hypoglycemia (Table 61.1)

| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Neonatal/juvenile/toy dog breed | Inadequate glycogen stores |
| Iatrogenic insulin overdose | Excess glucose utilization |
| Xylitol (dogs), ethanol, oral hypoglycemic agents, beta-blockers, alpha-lipoic acid | Various; usually hyperinsulinism |
| Refeeding syndrome | Excess glucose utilization due to hyperinsulinism |
| Malnutrition/starvation | Inadequate intake, depleted glycogen |
| Extreme exercise/hunting dog hypoglycemia | Excess utilization, inadequate stores |
| Insulinoma (common in dogs; less common in cats) | Hyperinsulinism |
| Extra-pancreatic neoplasia (dogs: hepatocellular carcinoma, hepatoma, leiomyosarcoma, leiomyoma; also cats) | Increased glucose utilization; insulin-like analogs |
| Severe infections (sepsis, babesiosis [dog], parvovirus) | Decreased hepatic gluconeogenesis, increased utilization |
| Hypoadrenocorticism (dogs and cats) | Decreased gluconeogenesis and counter-regulation |
| Severe liver disease (PSS, hepatitis, lipidosis, neoplasia, hepatotoxins) | Decreased hepatic gluconeogenesis |
| Chronic kidney failure | Decreased gluconeogenesis; impaired catecholamine counter-regulation |
| Hypothyroidism | Hyperinsulinism (reduced insulin clearance); decreased catecholamine counter-regulation |
| Islet cell hypertrophy/hyperplasia (nesidioblastosis) | Hyperinsulinism |
| Hyposomatotropism/panhypopituitarism | Decreased gluconeogenesis and counter-regulation |

#### Potential Causes of Hyperglycemia (Table 61.2)

| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Diabetes mellitus | Absolute or relative insulin deficiency |
| Stress hyperglycemia | Increased hepatic gluconeogenesis; counter-regulatory hormones |
| Postprandial (dogs) | Glucose absorption exceeds insulin secretory capacity |
| IV dextrose-containing fluids | Glucose delivery exceeds insulin secretory capacity |
| Hyperadrenocorticism / glucocorticoid treatment | Insulin resistance; predominantly via hepatic gluconeogenesis |
| Diestrus (bitch)/pregnancy/progestogen treatment | Insulin resistance due to progestogens and GH |
| Pancreatitis and pancreatic neoplasia | Absolute insulin deficiency |
| Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma | Insulin resistance from catecholamines |
| Renal failure | Urea suppresses insulin secretion; decreased capacity for glucosuric correction |
| Head trauma | Stress hyperglycemia |
| Thiazide diuretics | Hypokalemia → impaired K-dependent insulin release |

**Mild hyperglycemia**: 100–180 mg/mL (5–10 mmol/L) = typically clinically silent; may indicate subclinical DM ("pre-diabetes").

(Ch 61)

### Ch 62 — Blood Urea Nitrogen, Creatinine, and SDMA

#### Key Concepts and Non-renal Influences

**BUN:**
- 60–65% of filtered urea is reabsorbed proximally; additional reabsorption with ADH in collecting ducts.
- Non-renal increases: high-protein diet, GI hemorrhage, catabolic states (infection, prolonged exercise, rhabdomyolysis, fever, glucocorticoids, tissue necrosis, starvation).
- Non-renal decreases: hepatic insufficiency (PSS, cirrhosis, acute liver failure), polyuria.

**Creatinine (sCr):**
- Constant production from skeletal muscle creatine/phosphocreatine; production rate depends on muscle mass.
- Higher baseline in high-muscle-mass breeds (e.g., Greyhounds); lower in cachexia/sarcopenia.
- Thyroidal effects: untreated hypothyroid dogs → higher sCr; untreated hyperthyroid cats → lower sCr.
- **75% of functional renal mass must be lost** before significant changes in sCr (corresponds to ~48% decrease in GFR in dogs).

**SDMA:**
- Synthesized by all nucleated cells; >90% renally excreted by glomerular filtration.
- Less interindividual variability than sCr.
- SDMA rises with **20–40% reduction in GFR** — more sensitive than sCr.
- SDMA rises on average **9.8 months** (dogs) and **17 months** (cats) earlier than sCr in CKD patients.
- Minimal non-renal influences (not significantly affected by mitral regurgitation, pancreatitis, hyperthyroidism, muscle mass, age, sex, breed).

#### Azotemia Classification (Figure 62.1)

| Category | USG (Dog) | USG (Cat) | Key features |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-renal | >1.030 ("appropriate") | >1.035 | Hypovolemia, decreased cardiac output, altered vascular tone |
| Renal | 1.007–1.030 ("inappropriate") | 1.007–1.035 | Nephron loss, decreased glomerular patency |
| Post-renal | Variable | Variable | Obstruction or urine leakage; detected by imaging, fluid creatinine/K ratios |
| Isosthenuria | 1.008–1.012 | 1.008–1.012 | Neither concentrating nor diluting |

**Pre-renal causes:** Dehydration, shock, hemorrhage, GI losses (vomiting/diarrhea), third-spacing, hypoadrenocorticism; cardiomyopathies, tachyarrhythmias, bradyarrhythmias, sepsis/SIRS, anaphylaxis, hypoadrenocorticism; sepsis, SIRS, anaphylaxis.

**Renal causes:** CKD (glomerulonephritis, tubulointerstitial nephritis, amyloidosis, polycystic kidney disease, renal dysplasia, hydronephrosis, neoplasia); AKI (intoxications, leptospirosis, Lyme nephritis, pyelonephritis, sepsis/SIRS, ischemia).

**Post-renal causes (obstruction):** Ureteral calculi, ureteral ligation, TCC, urethral calculi, urethral plugs, urethral ligation, prostatic neoplasia, bladder herniation.

**Post-renal causes (urine leakage):** Blunt/penetrating trauma, iatrogenic procedural trauma, dehiscence after urinary surgery, non-traumatic rupture from obstruction, neoplasia.

#### Uroperitoneum Diagnostic Ratios
- **Fluid-to-blood creatinine ratio** usually >2:1 → 86% sensitivity, 100% specificity in dogs.
- **Fluid-to-blood potassium ratio** >1.4:1 (dogs) or >1.9:1 (cats) → 100% sensitivity and specificity for uroperitoneum.

(Ch 62)

### Ch 63 — Cholesterol and Triglycerides

#### Key Definitions and Thresholds
- **Lipemia** (grossly visible turbidity): typically triglycerides >200–300 mg/dL (>2.3–3.4 mmol/L)
- **Chylomicron test**: leave lipemic serum undisturbed at 4°C for 12h; cream layer = chylomicrons; turbid remaining serum = excess VLDL.
- **Post-prandial hyperlipidemia**: resolves within 7–12h after a meal; minimum 12h fast required before testing triglycerides/cholesterol.
- **Lipoprotein lipase activity test**: measure triglycerides before and 10 min after 40–90 IU/kg heparin IV; decrease in triglycerides = functional lipoprotein lipase.

#### Causes of Hyperlipidemia (Table 63.1)

| Cause | Lipid type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Postprandial | HTG ± HCH | Most common cause overall; lasts <15h |
| High-fat diet | HTG ± HCH | Fat content must typically be >50% |
| Diabetes mellitus* | HTG (mainly) ± HCH | >50% of cases; mild to marked |
| Hypothyroidism* | HTG ± HCH | >75% of cases; mild to marked |
| Hyperadrenocorticism* | HTG ± HCH | Mild to marked |
| Pancreatitis* | HTG ± HCH | ~30% of cases; typically mild |
| Obesity* | HTG ± HCH | >25% of cases |
| Protein-losing nephropathy* | HCH | Part of nephrotic syndrome; usually mild |
| Cholestasis* | HTG ± HCH | Usually mild |
| Hepatic insufficiency* | HTG ± HCH | Usually mild |
| Lymphoma | HTG ± HCH | May persist despite treatment |
| Leishmania infantum | HTG + HCH | Typically mild |
| Glucocorticoids | HTG ± HCH | Mild to marked |
| Phenobarbital | HTG | Dogs; mild to marked; >30% of cases |
| Megestrol acetate | HTG ± HCH | Mainly cats |
| Miniature Schnauzer (primary)* | HTG ± HCH | >30% of US dogs; prevalence increases with age |
| Beagle (primary)* | HTG ± HCH | Usually mild to moderate |
| Shetland Sheepdog (primary)* | HCH ± HTG | HCH may be marked; >40% in Japan |
| Cats — idiopathic hyperchylomicronemia (primary) | HTG | Decreased lipoprotein lipase; related colony cats |
| Cats — transient (kittens, primary) | HTG ± HCH | Often with anemia |
| Burmese cats (primary) | HTG | Usually normal fasting triglycerides; increased postprandial |

*Indicates common causes. \# indicates common causes in cats.

HCH = Hypercholesterolemia; HTG = Hypertriglyceridemia.

#### Consequences of Hyperlipidemia (Table 63.2)
| Disorder | Lipid type | Species |
|---|---|---|
| Pancreatitis | HTG | Dogs |
| Vacuolar hepatopathy | HTG | Dogs and cats |
| Hepatic lipidosis | HTG | Dogs and cats |
| Biliary mucocele | HTG/HCH | Dogs |
| Insulin resistance | HTG | Dogs and cats |
| Lipemia retinalis | HTG | Dogs and cats |
| Lipemic aqueous | HTG | Dogs and cats |
| Lipid keratopathy | HTG | Dogs and cats |
| Intraocular xanthogranuloma | HTG | Dogs (Mini Schnauzer) |
| Seizures | HTG | Dogs and cats |
| Lipomas | HTG | Dogs and cats |
| Atherosclerosis | HCH | Dogs and cats |
| Xanthomata | HTG | Dogs and cats |

#### Hypocholesterolemia and Hypotriglyceridemia
- **Hypocholesterolemia causes**: Protein-losing enteropathy (IBD, lymphoma, lymphangiectasia); hepatic insufficiency (cirrhosis, PSS); selected malignancies; severe caloric deficiency.
- **Hypotriglyceridemia**: Not clearly associated with any disease (possibly severe caloric deficiency).

(Ch 63)

### Ch 64 — Amylase and Lipase

#### Serum Amylase Activity
- **NOT clinically useful** for diagnosing pancreatitis: neither specific (amylase present after total pancreatectomy) nor sensitive. Increases in renal, hepatic, intestinal, and neoplastic disease.

#### Serum Lipase Assays — Comparison

| Assay | Substrate | Specificity | Utility |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,2-DiG-based | 1,2-diglyceride | Low (non-pancreatic lipases measured) | Historical; low sensitivity and specificity |
| DGGR-based (PSL, Antech) | DGGR | Moderate but not specific | Better than 1,2-DiG; heparin administration increases result (releases hepatic/lipoprotein lipases) |
| Triolein-based (V-Lip, Fuji) | Triolein | Limited (hemolysis/icterus interfere) | Only 58% EPI dogs have low 20th-percentile result |
| **PLI — Spec cPL/Spec fPL (IDEXX)** | Immunoassay (pancreatic lipase-specific) | **High** — analytically validated | Most sensitive/specific; gold standard |

**PLI key points:**
- cPLI is non-detectable/severely decreased in EPI dogs → confirms pancreatic origin.
- cPLI is NOT raised in experimentally induced renal disease → specific to pancreas.
- Spec cPL and Spec fPL are analytically validated (not all commercial PLI assays are).
- SNAP cPL/fPL (IDEXX): semiquantitative rapid rule-out. Normal = pancreatitis unlikely. Positive = pancreatitis possible or in "grey zone"; requires quantitative PLI for confirmation.
- Sensitivity varies widely (33–100% across studies); highest for acute severe disease; lower for chronic mild disease.
- Elevated PLI can occur with secondary pancreatic damage (cardiac, infectious, neurological, endocrine, renal diseases).

(Ch 64)

### Ch 65 — Liver Enzymes

#### Four Enzymes Used in Veterinary Practice
1. **ALT** — hepatocellular leakage enzyme
2. **AST** — hepatocellular leakage enzyme (also in skeletal muscle, cardiac, kidneys, brain, erythrocytes)
3. **ALP** — cholestatic enzyme (canalicular membrane)
4. **GGT** — cholestatic enzyme (canalicular membrane and microsomes)

#### ALT
- "Liver-specific" in dogs and cats; also in lesser amounts in heart, kidney, skeletal muscle.
- Half-life: 40–60 hours (dog); ~3–4 hours (cat).
- **Sensitivity**: 80–100% for hepatic necrosis/failure; 45–80% for hepatitis, cirrhosis, vacuolar hepatopathy, passive congestion, portovascular anomalies (dog).
- Cats: 80–100% sensitive for extrahepatic bile duct occlusion and cholangitis/cholangiohepatitis.
- Largest increases: necroinflammatory disease (drug/toxin, infectious, copper-associated hepatopathy, autoimmune).
- **Aflatoxin B1 exception**: inhibits biosynthesis of ALT and AST — not usable as biomarkers post-intoxication.
- Glucocorticoids in dogs: may induce ALT transcription but do not cause significant increases in cultured hepatocyte production.
- Cats: ALT may increase with hemolysis, hyperthyroidism, or rhabdomyolysis.

#### AST
- Greatest concentrations in skeletal muscle, cardiac myocytes, kidneys.
- Concurrent increase in CK = muscular source of AST elevation.
- Half-life: ~22 hours or longer (dog); ~77 minutes (cat).
- In cats, AST is more sensitive indicator of hepatocellular damage than ALT; most markedly increased in necroinflammatory diseases, infiltrative lymphoma, myeloproliferative disease, chronic bile duct obstruction.

#### ALP
- Dog: Two hepatic canalicular isoenzymes — L-ALP and G-ALP (glucocorticoid-induced, expressed from intestinal ALP gene).
  - G-ALP induced by exogenous glucocorticoids (delayed ~10 days), chronic diseases, anticonvulsants (phenobarbital).
  - L-ALP and G-ALP half-life: 2–3 days.
  - Feline L-ALP half-life: 6 hours (much shorter than dog → smaller magnitude of increase in cats is still significant).
- **Cats do NOT express G-ALP** → glucocorticoid therapy does not typically cause significant ALP elevation in cats.
- Bone ALP (B-ALP): present in growing dogs and cats up to 7 months; also in renal secondary hyperparathyroidism, bone tumors (negative prognostic sign for osteosarcoma), osteomyelitis, feline hyperthyroidism.
- High sensitivity but **low specificity** for hepatobiliary disease (dog); high specificity when concurrent GGT also elevated.
- **Scottish Terriers**: breed-related hyperphosphatasemia; associated with G-ALP, progressive vacuolar hepatopathy, adrenal dysfunction, hepatocellular carcinoma.
- Cats: ALP increase in hepatic lipidosis often predominates; also intrahepatic/extrahepatic biliary injury.

#### GGT
- Dog: largest tissue concentration in proximal renal tubules and pancreas (lost into urine/pancreatic lumen rather than circulation → low serum GGT from these sources).
- **Sensitivity (dog)**: ~40% for liver disease — not sensitive; **higher specificity** than ALP.
- **Cats**: Sensitivity 55%; ALP exceeds GGT specificity in cats; GGT most markedly increased in necroinflammatory diseases of portal tract, biliary tree, and pancreas.
- Both ALP and GGT elevated: more likely to be true liver disease.
- Extrahepatic bile duct obstruction: moderate to severe GGT increases (generally greater in dogs than cats).
- GGT NOT significantly elevated in simple hepatic lipidosis (unlike ALP which increases markedly).
- Neonatal dogs: markedly increased GGT for first 1–3 days due to colostrum.

#### Non-Hepatic Causes of Increased Liver Enzymes (Table 65.1)
| Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Cardiovascular | Congestion, hypotension, ischemia |
| Endocrinopathies | Adrenal (cortisol/sex steroid excess), DM, hyperthyroidism (cats), hypothyroidism (dogs) |
| GI disease | Diarrhea, constipation/obstipation, GDV, pancreatitis |
| Infectious disease | Abscessation, rickettsial, pyelonephritis, pyometra/prostatitis, septicemia, parvovirus, coronavirus |
| Miscellaneous | Strenuous exercise, trauma, myopathies, severe anemia, malignant hyperthermia |
| Neoplasia | Bone, mammary, metastatic |
| Osseous | Growth, metabolic bone disease, osteomyelitis |

#### Hepatotoxic Drug List (Box 65.1)
Acetaminophen, amiodarone, anabolic steroids, azathioprine, carprofen, cyclosporine, diazepam, diethylcarbamazine/oxibendazole, fluoroquinolones, griseofulvin, halothane, itraconazole, ketoconazole, lomustine (CCNU), mebendazole, methimazole, mibolerone, pennyroyal oil, phenobarbital, sulfonamides, tetracyclines.

#### Monitoring Parameters
- Following acute hepatic injury: transaminases rise within 24–48h, begin to decrease within 2–3 days, normalize in 2–3 weeks.
- Waxing and waning values: suggest chronic inflammatory condition.
- Reduction in enzyme activity in chronic liver disease may reflect improvement OR loss of hepatocytes.

(Ch 65)
